title: Mathematical Methods for Economics
subject: Economics

cards.prompt: What is Economic Variable? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An economic variable is a quantity that can vary within a model, such as a choice, price, or output. Whether it is endogenous or exogenous depends on what the model determines rather than on the quantity's name alone.
required_concepts: Variable role depends on the model boundary.
major_error_concepts: Assuming price must be endogenous in every model regardless of whether it is taken as given.

cards.prompt: What is Parameter? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A parameter describes a fixed feature during a particular model calculation, such as a technology coefficient or preference weight. Comparative statics can vary a parameter across otherwise specified problems.
required_concepts: Fixed within one problem but variable across comparisons.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a parameter can never be estimated or varied because it is held fixed in one calculation.

cards.prompt: What is Function and Correspondence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function assigns one output to each input in its domain. An economic correspondence may instead assign several possible outcomes, so nonunique optimal choices need not define a single-valued function.
required_concepts: One output per input; correspondences can be set-valued.
major_error_concepts: Calling a nonunique choice relation single-valued without a selection rule.

cards.prompt: What is Domain and Range? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function's domain is the set of inputs for which its definition applies, while its range consists of attained outputs. Economic restrictions such as nonnegative consumption are part of the domain, not optional decorations.
required_concepts: Allowed inputs and attained outputs distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Optimizing over negative quantities excluded by the stated economic domain.

cards.prompt: What is Implicit Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An implicit relation F(x,y)=0 defines linked variables without necessarily isolating one as an explicit function of the other. A local explicit solution requires suitable conditions and may fail or have multiple branches.
required_concepts: Equation-defined relation need not globally define one function.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every equilibrium equation has exactly one globally defined solution branch.

cards.prompt: What is Level Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A level set collects inputs giving the same function value. Examples include isoquants and indifference sets, but their economic interpretation depends on the function and whether increasing transformations preserve the intended ranking.
required_concepts: Inputs sharing one output level.
major_error_concepts: Equating a level set with the set of all values above that level.

cards.prompt: What is Sets and Feasibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Set operations describe feasible collections: intersection imposes conditions together, union allows membership in either set, and complement depends on a specified universe. Optimization requires preserving these logical distinctions.
required_concepts: Intersection versus union reflects joint versus alternative conditions.
major_error_concepts: Replacing intersecting constraints by their union and claiming the feasible set is unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Intervals and Bounds? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An interval describes allowed scalar values and whether endpoints are included. Closed bounded intervals are compact in the real line, supporting existence results for continuous objectives, unlike arbitrary open or unbounded domains.
required_concepts: Endpoint inclusion and boundedness matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a continuous objective must attain a maximum on every open interval.

cards.prompt: What is Summation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Summation notation adds indexed quantities over a stated index set. Index definitions, units, and whether a sum counts each item or pair once matter in economic aggregation.
required_concepts: Indexed addition with clear counting and units.
major_error_concepts: Counting every pair twice while interpreting the sum as a once-per-pair total.

cards.prompt: What is Sequence and Series? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sequence is an ordered list indexed by discrete time or another countable index. Its limiting behavior and cumulative sum are different questions; a sequence can approach zero while its infinite sum still diverges.
required_concepts: Indexed values with distinct limit and summability questions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming terms approaching zero automatically guarantee a convergent infinite series.

cards.prompt: What is Growth Rate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A proportional growth rate describes change relative to the current level. Discrete growth uses ratios between dates, while continuous instantaneous growth is xdot/x when x is positive and differentiable.
required_concepts: Relative rather than absolute change, with time convention stated.
major_error_concepts: Calling a fixed absolute increment the same percentage growth at every level.

cards.prompt: What is Compounding? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Discrete compounding multiplies a balance by one plus the per-period rate each period, giving X_t=X_0(1+r)^t for constant r. Continuous compounding uses exp(r t), with the rate convention and time unit kept explicit.
required_concepts: Multiplicative accumulation with discrete versus continuous convention.
major_error_concepts: Using an annual rate as a monthly rate without converting the period convention.

cards.prompt: What is Discount Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Discounting converts a dated payoff into a value at a reference date using the model's discount factors. For a constant discrete rate r it divides by (1+r)^t; this is a valuation convention under assumptions, not a prediction that every future payoff is certain.
required_concepts: Time-indexed valuation with specified discount factor.
major_error_concepts: Treating discounting alone as removal of uncertainty about whether a payoff occurs.

cards.prompt: What is Annuity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A level annuity is a finite sequence of equal periodic payments. Its present value is the sum of each payment times its date-specific discount factor, with payment timing and any constant-rate shortcut stated.
required_concepts: Sum discounted equal payments with explicit dates.
major_error_concepts: Using an end-of-period formula unchanged for payments beginning immediately without a timing adjustment.

cards.prompt: What is Limit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A limit describes the value approached by a function or sequence as its argument approaches a specified point or regime. Existence of a limit does not require the function value at the point to equal it or even be defined.
required_concepts: Approached value distinguished from point value.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a removable missing value prevents the surrounding limit from existing.

cards.prompt: What is Continuity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function is continuous at a point when its limiting value there equals its defined value. Continuity supports stable local response and existence arguments, but does not imply differentiability or monotonicity.
required_concepts: Limit equals function value at the point.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every continuous function has a derivative everywhere.

cards.prompt: What is Derivative? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A derivative measures local output change per small input change, where the limit exists. In economics it often represents a marginal quantity, but its units and held-fixed conditions must follow the model.
required_concepts: Local marginal rate of change.
major_error_concepts: Equating average cost with marginal cost solely because both describe cost behavior.

cards.prompt: What is Partial Derivative? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A partial derivative changes one independent input while holding the other specified inputs fixed. It differs from a total response when those other inputs themselves adjust endogenously.
required_concepts: Single-input derivative with other coordinates fixed.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a partial derivative as a full equilibrium response when other variables move.

cards.prompt: What is Total Differential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The total differential df=sum f_i dx_i gives the first-order response to changes in several inputs. It is a local linear approximation to finite changes, not generally the exact change in a nonlinear function.
required_concepts: Sum of sensitivity times input changes.
major_error_concepts: Using the linear differential as an exact finite change for every nonlinear model.

cards.prompt: What is Chain Rule? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The chain rule accounts for indirect dependence through intermediate variables. If y=f(x(a),a), dy/da=f_x dx/da+f_a, distinguishing the induced x response from the direct parameter effect.
required_concepts: Direct plus indirect derivative contributions.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the optimizer or equilibrium variable's dependence on a parameter when computing its total outcome response.

cards.prompt: What is Implicit Function Derivative? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For F(x,a)=0 with nonzero F_x and appropriate smoothness, a local solution satisfies dx/da=-F_a/F_x. The nonzero derivative condition is essential and does not establish global uniqueness across the entire parameter range.
required_concepts: Local implicit derivative with nonzero denominator.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by zero at a singular equilibrium and claiming the same local theorem applies.

cards.prompt: What is Elasticity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The elasticity of y=f(x) with respect to x is (dy/dx)(x/y) where defined. It measures proportional output change per proportional input change and is dimensionless, unlike an unscaled slope.
required_concepts: Derivative times input-output ratio.
major_error_concepts: Comparing slopes measured in different units as if they were elasticities.

cards.prompt: What is the logarithmic derivative of a differentiable, nonzero function y=f(x), and how does it relate to elasticity?
cards.definition: On an interval where f is differentiable and nonzero, its logarithmic derivative is f'(x)/f(x)=d ln|f(x)|/dx. Multiplying by x gives the point elasticity x f'(x)/f(x). When x and f(x) are positive, that elasticity is d ln f(x)/d ln x; it is not the unscaled logarithmic derivative.
required_concepts: Logarithmic derivative is f'/f=d ln|f|/dx where f is differentiable and nonzero.
Elasticity is x times the logarithmic derivative; the ordinary real log-log expression requires positive arguments.
accepted_variants: The proportional rate of change per unit of x is y'/y; the proportional response per proportional change of x is x y'/y.
major_error_concepts: Identifying f'/f with x f'/f for arbitrary x.
Taking ln f over negative values without using ln|f| or stating another domain convention.

cards.prompt: What is Second Derivative? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A second derivative measures how a marginal effect changes with its input. Its sign characterizes local curvature in one dimension, not whether the original function itself is positive or negative.
required_concepts: Change in the marginal effect and curvature.
major_error_concepts: Inferring negative function values from a negative second derivative alone.

cards.prompt: What is Taylor Expansion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Taylor expansion approximates a smooth function near a reference point using derivatives and a remainder. The expansion's usefulness depends on the size of the change and control of neglected higher-order terms.
required_concepts: Local derivative expansion with remainder.
major_error_concepts: Treating a local quadratic approximation as globally exact for an arbitrary objective.

cards.prompt: What is Stationary Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A stationary point has zero first derivative or gradient in an unconstrained differentiable interior problem. It may be a maximum, minimum, or saddle, and constrained or boundary optima need not be stationary in the unrestricted sense.
required_concepts: Zero gradient is an interior candidate condition, not a complete optimum test.
major_error_concepts: Declaring every zero-gradient point a maximum.

cards.prompt: What is Second-Derivative Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In one dimension, a negative second derivative at a stationary point gives a strict local maximum and a positive one gives a strict local minimum. A zero second derivative makes this test inconclusive rather than proving no optimum exists.
required_concepts: Curvature test at a stationary point with zero case inconclusive.
major_error_concepts: Calling zero second derivative proof of neither a maximum nor a minimum.

cards.prompt: What is Convex Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A convex set contains every line segment joining two of its points. It describes feasibility geometry and differs from convexity of an objective function defined over that set.
required_concepts: All convex combinations remain feasible.
major_error_concepts: Calling a set convex merely because its objective is convex.

cards.prompt: What is Convex Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A convex function lies below or on chords connecting its graph points over a convex domain. Convex minimization has useful global properties, while maximizing a convex function is not the same easy optimization class.
required_concepts: Function value at mixture no greater than mixture of values.
major_error_concepts: Assuming convexity guarantees any stationary point is a global maximum.

cards.prompt: What is Concave Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A concave function lies above or on chords over its convex domain. Maximizing a concave objective over a convex feasible set supports global optimality conditions, but increasing transformations need not preserve concavity.
required_concepts: Mixture value at least mixture of values.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every increasing transformation of a concave utility function remains concave.

cards.prompt: What is Strict Convexity and Concavity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Strict convexity or concavity makes the relevant chord inequality strict for distinct points and interior mixtures. It can give uniqueness of an attained optimum in the corresponding convex optimization problem, but does not itself guarantee existence on an arbitrary domain.
required_concepts: Strict chord inequality supports uniqueness if optimum exists.
major_error_concepts: Claiming strict concavity alone guarantees an attained maximum on every unbounded domain.

cards.prompt: What is Quasiconcavity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A quasiconcave function has convex upper-level sets, allowing preference-convexity reasoning without requiring concavity of its numerical representation. Increasing transformations preserve quasiconcavity but not necessarily ordinary concavity.
required_concepts: Convex upper contour sets, weaker than concavity.
major_error_concepts: Equating quasiconcavity with a negative-definite Hessian everywhere.

cards.prompt: What is Hessian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function. With continuous second derivatives it is symmetric, and its quadratic form describes second-order changes around a point.
required_concepts: Second-partial derivative matrix with curvature role.
major_error_concepts: Using only separate diagonal second derivatives while ignoring mixed curvature in a multivariable problem.

cards.prompt: What is Semidefinite Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when x transpose A x is nonnegative for every vector x. Negative semidefiniteness reverses the inequality; zero directions are permitted and can leave strict local tests inconclusive.
required_concepts: Quadratic form sign for every vector, allowing zeros.
major_error_concepts: Checking only positive diagonal entries and concluding the whole matrix is positive semidefinite.

cards.prompt: What is Definite Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A symmetric matrix is positive definite when its quadratic form is positive for every nonzero vector. Negative definite curvature at an unconstrained stationary point gives a strict local maximum, while positive definite curvature gives a strict local minimum.
required_concepts: Strict quadratic-form sign on nonzero directions.
major_error_concepts: Confusing negative determinant alone with negative definiteness in every dimension.

cards.prompt: What is Principal-Minor Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a symmetric matrix, Sylvester's criterion uses positive leading principal minors to establish positive definiteness. Negative definiteness has alternating leading-minor signs after the corresponding sign transformation; semidefiniteness requires different care.
required_concepts: Leading-minor sign criterion for definite symmetric matrices.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same leading-minors-only rule blindly to positive semidefiniteness.

cards.prompt: What is Unconstrained Optimality Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a differentiable interior unconstrained optimum, the objective gradient is zero. This necessary condition must be followed by curvature or global arguments and does not apply unchanged when the optimum is on a binding boundary.
required_concepts: Interior first-order gradient condition.
major_error_concepts: Rejecting a valid boundary optimum because its unrestricted gradient is nonzero.

cards.prompt: What is Second-Order Optimality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Second-order optimality tests examine the objective Hessian at a stationary point, or an appropriate constrained curvature expression. Negative definiteness is sufficient for a strict unconstrained local maximum, while semidefinite cases can need higher-order analysis.
required_concepts: Curvature refines stationary-point classification.
major_error_concepts: Declaring every negative-semidefinite stationary Hessian proof of a strict maximum.

cards.prompt: What is Local and Global Optima? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A global maximum is at least as good as every feasible alternative, while a local maximum only dominates nearby alternatives. Concavity over a convex domain can convert suitable local maximum conditions into global conclusions.
required_concepts: All feasible alternatives versus nearby alternatives.
major_error_concepts: Calling a locally fitted or locally stationary solution globally optimal without the needed argument.

cards.prompt: What is Boundary Optimum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A boundary optimum lies where one or more feasibility restrictions bind. Feasible directional changes, not every unrestricted direction, determine its optimality, so interior tangency equations alone can miss it.
required_concepts: Optimize over feasible directions at active boundaries.
major_error_concepts: Discarding a boundary solution solely because the objective derivative does not vanish.

cards.prompt: What is Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A constraint restricts choices through equalities, inequalities, or domain membership. Its mathematical sign convention determines multiplier signs in later optimality conditions and must remain consistent.
required_concepts: Explicit feasible-choice restriction with sign convention.
major_error_concepts: Reversing an inequality without changing multiplier conventions in the resulting KKT system.

cards.prompt: What is Feasible Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The feasible set contains all choices satisfying every model constraint simultaneously. A candidate objective value is irrelevant to admissible optimization if its associated choice violates the feasible set.
required_concepts: Intersection of all applicable restrictions.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an infeasible higher objective as the solution to the constrained problem.

cards.prompt: What is Existence of an Optimum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A continuous objective on a nonempty compact feasible set attains both maximum and minimum. This existence result does not guarantee uniqueness or provide a method for locating the optimizer by itself.
required_concepts: Continuity plus nonempty compactness gives attainment.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the theorem provides a unique optimum or applies unchanged to every open feasible set.

cards.prompt: What is Lagrangian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Lagrangian combines an objective with multiplier-weighted constraints under a chosen convention. For maximizing f subject to g(x)=b, one convention is L=f+lambda(b-g), linking stationarity to constrained tradeoffs.
required_concepts: Objective plus consistently signed constraint terms.
major_error_concepts: Using a multiplier interpretation from the opposite sign convention without conversion.

cards.prompt: What is Lagrange Multiplier? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Lagrange multiplier can measure the local change in optimized value when its constraint limit relaxes, under regularity and a compatible sign convention. Its units follow objective units per constraint-bound unit.
required_concepts: Local shadow value of constraint relaxation under stated conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every multiplier is automatically positive or measured in currency regardless of convention and objective.

cards.prompt: What is Constrained Tangency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At a regular equality-constrained interior optimum, the objective gradient lies in the span of active constraint gradients. This expresses zero first-order gain along feasible tangent directions, not zero unrestricted objective gradient in general.
required_concepts: Gradient alignment removes gains along feasible tangents.
major_error_concepts: Demanding unrestricted gradient zero at every constrained optimum.

cards.prompt: What is KKT Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: KKT conditions combine stationarity, primal feasibility, dual sign feasibility, and complementary slackness for inequality-constrained optimization. Constraint qualification supports necessity, while convexity or concavity assumptions can support sufficiency under the correct formulation.
required_concepts: All four KKT components with conditions for interpretation.
major_error_concepts: Treating KKT as globally sufficient for every nonconvex problem without additional assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Complementary Slackness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Complementary slackness requires each inequality multiplier times its constraint slack to equal zero in the KKT system. A strictly slack constraint has zero multiplier, but a binding constraint can also have zero multiplier in a degenerate case.
required_concepts: Multiplier-slack product zero.
Binding need not imply strictly positive multiplier.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every binding constraint necessarily has a nonzero shadow price.

cards.prompt: What is Constraint Qualification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A constraint qualification is a regularity condition permitting valid multiplier-based necessary conditions at a local optimum. It differs from curvature assumptions that can make those conditions globally sufficient.
required_concepts: Regularity enables multiplier representation.
Distinct from sufficiency curvature.
major_error_concepts: Using concavity alone as proof that every singular constraint representation admits ordinary multipliers.

cards.prompt: What is Optimization Duality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optimization duality constructs an auxiliary multiplier problem whose value bounds the primal problem under the chosen formulation. Equality of primal and dual values is strong duality and needs appropriate conditions; it is not automatic for all problems.
required_concepts: Dual bounds and conditional primal-dual equality.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero duality gap for every arbitrary nonconvex program.

cards.prompt: What is Envelope Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The envelope theorem differentiates an optimized value through direct parameter effects, including constraint effects through the appropriate Lagrangian, when regularity holds. It can avoid differentiating the optimizer explicitly but does not erase parameter-dependent constraints.
required_concepts: Optimized-value derivative from direct Lagrangian parameter effect.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring a moving budget constraint while differentiating only the raw objective's explicit parameter dependence.

cards.prompt: What is Comparative Statics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Comparative statics studies how equilibrium or optimal choices change when parameters change. It uses local derivatives or global comparisons with existence and selection assumptions, rather than automatically describing the time path between equilibria.
required_concepts: Parameter-driven comparison of model outcomes, not adjustment dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Inferring transition speed solely from the sign of a comparative-static derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Monotone Transformation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A strictly increasing transformation of an objective preserves every ranking and the entire set of maximizers over the same feasible set. It can change curvature, marginal units, and multipliers. A merely nondecreasing transformation can collapse distinct values into ties and introduce additional maximizers.
required_concepts: Strictly increasing on the objective's attained range, with the same feasible set, preserves rankings and the argmax set.
Curvature and numerical derivatives need not be preserved.
accepted_variants: An order-preserving scalar reindexing keeps ordinal choices but not the objective's cardinal derivative scale.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every nondecreasing transformation preserves the exact argmax set.
Claiming a strictly increasing transformation preserves all marginal utilities or multipliers numerically.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function is homogeneous of degree k when f(t x)=t^k f(x) for positive scale t on a suitable cone domain. Homogeneity describes joint scaling of all inputs, not arbitrary changes in one input alone.
required_concepts: Joint input scaling produces degree-k output scaling.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a degree from changing one factor while the other inputs stay fixed.

cards.prompt: What is Euler Homogeneity Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a differentiable degree-k homogeneous function, Euler's theorem gives sum x_i partial f/partial x_i=k f(x). It requires homogeneity and differentiability on the relevant domain, not just any smooth production function.
required_concepts: Input-weighted marginal products sum to k times output.
major_error_concepts: Applying the identity without establishing the function's degree of homogeneity.

cards.prompt: What is Homotheticity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Homothetic preferences can be represented under standard conditions by an increasing transformation of a degree-one homogeneous function. Their indifference sets scale radially, and unique demands scale with income at fixed prices on the suitable domain.
required_concepts: Radially scaled preference contours via monotone homogeneous representation.
major_error_concepts: Equating homotheticity with a requirement that the displayed utility function itself be linear.

cards.prompt: What is Returns to Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Returns to scale compare output when all production inputs are multiplied together. A homogeneous production function has constant, increasing, or decreasing returns according as its degree equals, exceeds, or falls below one over the modeled scale domain.
required_concepts: Joint-input scaling and homogeneous degree classification.
major_error_concepts: Confusing diminishing marginal product of one input with decreasing returns to scaling every input.

cards.prompt: What is Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A matrix represents a linear map between vector coordinates once bases are chosen. Economic uses include systems of market equations, input-output relations, and local derivatives, with dimensions determining compatible operations.
required_concepts: Linear mapping with explicit row-column dimensions.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying dimensionally incompatible matrices while treating the result as a valid transformation.

cards.prompt: What is Matrix Multiplication? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Matrix multiplication composes compatible linear maps and generally does not commute. In a product ABx, B acts on x first under the usual column-vector convention.
required_concepts: Composition order B then A in ABx.
major_error_concepts: Reordering factors freely as if matrix multiplication were ordinary scalar multiplication.

cards.prompt: What is Determinant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A determinant is a scalar associated with a square matrix that indicates signed volume scaling. A nonzero determinant identifies an invertible finite-dimensional linear map, while zero indicates dependence and loss of invertibility.
required_concepts: Square-matrix signed volume scale and singularity criterion.
major_error_concepts: Treating determinant zero as proof that every associated linear system has no solution rather than possible nonuniqueness.

cards.prompt: What is Matrix Inverse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The inverse of a nonsingular square matrix reverses its linear action, satisfying A inverse A=I and A A inverse=I. An inverse is useful for algebraic characterization, though direct numerical solves can be preferable to explicitly forming it.
required_concepts: Two-sided inverse exists for nonsingular square maps.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every rectangular or singular matrix has an ordinary two-sided inverse.

cards.prompt: What is Rank? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Rank is the dimension of a matrix's column space, equal to its row-space dimension. It measures independent linear information and helps distinguish redundant equations from genuinely independent constraints.
required_concepts: Dimension of independent column or row information.
major_error_concepts: Counting every written equation as independent without considering linear dependence.

cards.prompt: What is Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear system Ax=b has a solution when b lies in A's column space, and uniqueness additionally requires a trivial null space for the unknowns. A square nonsingular system has the unique solution A inverse b.
required_concepts: Range condition for existence and null-space condition for uniqueness.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the same number of equations and unknowns guarantees nonsingularity.

cards.prompt: What is Eigenvalue and Eigenvector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector v satisfying Av=lambda v. The eigenvalue describes scaling along that invariant direction and helps analyze repeated linear economic dynamics.
required_concepts: Nonzero invariant-direction vector and scaling value.
major_error_concepts: Allowing the zero vector as an eigenvector for every lambda.

cards.prompt: What is Spectral Radius? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Spectral radius is the largest absolute eigenvalue of a square matrix. For a finite-dimensional linear discrete system x_(t+1)=A x_t, spectral radius below one gives convergence to zero from every initial state.
required_concepts: Maximum eigenvalue magnitude and discrete linear stability condition.
major_error_concepts: Checking only whether real eigenvalues are less than one while ignoring negative magnitude or complex eigenvalues.

cards.prompt: What is Quadratic Form? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A quadratic form x transpose A x measures direction-dependent curvature when A is symmetric. It connects Hessian analysis, matrix definiteness, and local changes in multivariable objectives.
required_concepts: Scalar quadratic matrix expression and curvature role.
major_error_concepts: Inferring its sign from one chosen direction rather than all directions required for definiteness.

cards.prompt: What is Input-Output Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple input-output model writes gross output x=A x+d, where A contains input requirements and d is final demand. When the relevant productivity conditions hold, x=(I-A) inverse d; algebraic invertibility alone does not guarantee every economically desired nonnegative property.
required_concepts: Gross output covers intermediate and final demand.
major_error_concepts: Treating any invertible coefficient matrix as automatically a feasible productive nonnegative economy.

cards.prompt: What is Transition Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A row-stochastic transition matrix has nonnegative entries and each row sums to one. A row-vector state distribution evolves as p_next=p P under that convention; column-vector conventions require the corresponding transpose arrangement.
required_concepts: Nonnegative row probabilities sum to one with matching vector convention.
major_error_concepts: Mixing a row-stochastic matrix with an incompatible column update and assuming probabilities remain normalized.

cards.prompt: What is Gradient? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The gradient of a scalar function collects its first partial derivatives into a vector under a declared convention. Its dot product with a small direction gives first-order change, supporting feasible-direction optimization reasoning.
required_concepts: Vector of marginal derivatives and directional change.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a gradient vector with the Hessian matrix of second derivatives.

cards.prompt: What is Jacobian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Jacobian matrix collects first partial derivatives of a vector-valued function. It gives a local linear approximation to simultaneous equations and is distinct from the Hessian of one scalar objective.
required_concepts: Derivative matrix of a vector-valued map.
major_error_concepts: Calling every Jacobian symmetric as though it were a smooth scalar Hessian.

cards.prompt: What is Multivariate Implicit Function Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For equilibrium equations F(x,a)=0 with an invertible Jacobian F_x, the local response is dx/da=-F_x inverse F_a under appropriate smoothness. The result is local and can fail at singular points or branch changes.
required_concepts: Matrix implicit response requires invertible equilibrium Jacobian.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula through a singular Jacobian without checking whether a differentiable local branch exists.

cards.prompt: What is Antiderivative? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An antiderivative F satisfies F prime=f on an interval. It is defined up to an additive constant, which can encode an initial stock or baseline when integrating a marginal economic quantity.
required_concepts: Function with specified derivative plus constant freedom.
major_error_concepts: Recovering total cost from marginal cost while silently forcing the fixed-cost constant to zero.

cards.prompt: What is Definite Integral? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A definite integral accumulates a quantity over an interval with an orientation and measure. Integrating a flow over time gives a stock change only when the flow and units describe the relevant accumulation correctly.
required_concepts: Signed interval accumulation with appropriate units.
major_error_concepts: Treating every area under a plotted curve as the same economic quantity regardless of axis units.

cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Theorem of Calculus? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The fundamental theorem of calculus connects accumulation and marginal change: integrating a derivative gives endpoint differences under appropriate regularity. It supports recovering changes in total quantities from their marginal functions.
required_concepts: Integral of derivative equals endpoint difference under conditions.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring an unknown integration constant when claiming an absolute total from marginal data alone.

cards.prompt: What is Integration by Parts? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Integration by parts transfers a derivative between factors while retaining the endpoint term: integral u dv=uv minus integral v du. Endpoint conditions determine whether the boundary contribution vanishes.
required_concepts: Product-rule integration with boundary term.
major_error_concepts: Dropping endpoint terms automatically in a discounted or intertemporal calculation.

cards.prompt: What is Integration by Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Substitution changes integration variables with the appropriate derivative or Jacobian factor and transformed bounds. Economic variable transformations must also preserve the feasible domain and units.
required_concepts: Transform measure, bounds, and domain consistently.
major_error_concepts: Changing only the variable name while omitting the scaling factor.

cards.prompt: What is Consumer-Surplus Integral? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the standard partial-equilibrium welfare interpretation, consumer surplus is the area under inverse demand above the paid price for purchased units. Its welfare use is exact only under suitable assumptions about income effects or the valuation model.
required_concepts: Demand-based willingness-to-pay area net of expenditure.
major_error_concepts: Treating the area as a universally exact welfare measure under arbitrary income effects without qualification.

cards.prompt: What is Producer-Surplus Integral? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Producer surplus is revenue minus relevant variable cost in the standard competitive supply interpretation. Integrating marginal cost constructs variable cost up to the chosen baseline, while fixed costs distinguish surplus from total economic profit.
required_concepts: Revenue above variable cost, with fixed costs treated separately.
major_error_concepts: Equating producer surplus with profit regardless of fixed costs.

cards.prompt: What is Expectation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An expectation is a probability-weighted average of a random variable, defined by a sum or integral when it exists. It need not equal the most likely outcome or be an actually attainable discrete outcome.
required_concepts: Probability-weighted mean with existence conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the expected payoff must be the outcome observed most often.

cards.prompt: What is Random Variable? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A random variable maps outcomes to numerical quantities, with its distribution specifying probabilities. Its realized value and its full probability law are different objects, both relevant to decisions under uncertainty.
required_concepts: Numerical outcome mapping and separate distribution.
major_error_concepts: Equating one observed realization with the complete distribution of possible outcomes.

cards.prompt: What is Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Variance is the expected squared deviation from a variable's mean when finite. It measures dispersion in squared units and does not alone describe tail shape or every economically relevant risk.
required_concepts: Expected squared centered deviation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming identical variances imply identical distributions or every same risk characteristic.

cards.prompt: What is Covariance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Covariance measures joint centered variation between two variables. It affects the variance of sums and portfolios in an academic model, and zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
required_concepts: Joint centered variation and sum-variance role.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring covariance when adding risks of dependent quantities.

cards.prompt: What is Conditional Expectation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Conditional expectation averages a random quantity given specified information. It is itself a function of that information before realization and need not equal the unconditional mean.
required_concepts: Information-conditioned mean.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the conditioning information and assuming the expected value remains unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Bayes Rule? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Bayes' rule updates a prior probability using likelihood and positive-probability evidence through normalization. The probability of data given a hypothesis is not the same as the probability of that hypothesis given the data.
required_concepts: Posterior proportional to likelihood times prior with normalization.
major_error_concepts: Reversing conditional probabilities without accounting for prior and evidence.

cards.prompt: What is Jensen Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Jensen's inequality states that for a convex function phi, phi(E[X]) is at most E[phi(X)] when the quantities are defined. Concavity reverses the inequality, linking curvature to evaluation of risk.
required_concepts: Convex function of mean no greater than mean of function.
major_error_concepts: Assuming nonlinear transformation commutes with expectation in general.

cards.prompt: What is Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds an inner product's magnitude by the product of norms. Applied to centered random variables with finite variances, it bounds absolute covariance by the product of standard deviations.
required_concepts: Inner-product bound and covariance consequence.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a covariance can exceed both standard deviations' product while retaining a valid finite-variance joint distribution.

cards.prompt: What is Difference Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A difference equation relates values across discrete periods, such as x_(t+1)=f(x_t). Its timing convention determines how initial conditions and parameter changes propagate through the sequence.
required_concepts: Discrete-time state update.
major_error_concepts: Treating a difference equation as an instantaneous derivative without specifying a limiting approximation.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Difference Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A first-order affine difference equation is x_(t+1)=a x_t+b. When a differs from one its fixed point is b/(1-a), and deviations follow multiplication by a each period.
required_concepts: Affine update and geometric deviation dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Using the fixed-point formula at a=1 without considering the special case.

cards.prompt: What is Steady State? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A discrete-time steady state satisfies x_star=f(x_star). It is unchanged by the update rule, but existence of that point does not establish that nearby trajectories converge to it.
required_concepts: Fixed point of the state update.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every steady state is attracting merely because it solves the equilibrium equation.

cards.prompt: What is Discrete-Time Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a differentiable scalar discrete map near a fixed point, absolute derivative below one gives local attraction and above one gives local repulsion under standard conditions. Magnitude equal to one requires further analysis.
required_concepts: Discrete stability uses absolute derivative relative to one.
accepted_variants: Local stability of a difference equation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a derivative of minus two stable merely because it is less than one algebraically.

cards.prompt: What is Periodic Orbit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A periodic orbit of a discrete map returns to its initial state after a finite number of updates. A period-k orbit is distinct from a fixed point when k is the smallest positive return time greater than one.
required_concepts: Finite repeated state sequence with minimal period.
major_error_concepts: Calling every oscillating-looking transient an exact periodic orbit.

cards.prompt: What is Differential Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ordinary differential equation models continuous-time change through derivatives, such as xdot=f(x,t). Initial conditions select trajectories when the equation satisfies suitable existence and uniqueness assumptions.
required_concepts: Continuous-time derivative evolution with initial data.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every arbitrary discontinuous differential equation has a unique trajectory from every initial point.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Continuous Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The scalar continuous-time equation xdot=a x+b has exponential deviation from a fixed point when one exists. Stability requires a negative growth coefficient a, unlike the absolute-less-than-one criterion for a discrete-time multiplier.
required_concepts: Continuous affine dynamics with negative-rate stability.
major_error_concepts: Applying the discrete |a|<1 criterion directly to a continuous-time rate.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Diagram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A phase diagram shows the direction of state change and equilibrium structure rather than only state values against calendar time. In one dimension the sign of xdot on either side of a fixed point indicates attraction or repulsion when the local model is regular.
required_concepts: State-dependent direction-of-motion diagram.
major_error_concepts: Inferring stability from equilibrium location alone without examining nearby flow directions.

cards.prompt: What is Dynamical System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A dynamical system evolves several state variables together through a vector difference or differential equation. Coupling means each component's trajectory may depend on the others, so independent one-variable solutions may not describe the system.
required_concepts: Coupled multivariable state evolution.
major_error_concepts: Dropping cross-variable effects while claiming to solve the original coupled system exactly.

cards.prompt: What is Dynamic Linearization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linearization approximates a smooth nonlinear system near an equilibrium using its Jacobian there. Nonmarginal eigenvalues determine local behavior under appropriate conditions; zero real parts or unit-modulus discrete eigenvalues can require nonlinear analysis.
required_concepts: Jacobian local approximation with marginal-case limits.
major_error_concepts: Treating the linearized approximation as a global solution across arbitrarily large state changes.

cards.prompt: What is Saddle-Path Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A saddle equilibrium has both locally attracting and repelling directions in the relevant dynamical description. A stable path can approach it from restricted initial states even though generic nearby perturbations diverge in other directions.
required_concepts: Mixed stable and unstable directions.
major_error_concepts: Calling a saddle globally attracting because one selected path converges to it.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous Discounting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Continuous discounting weights a payoff at time t by exp(-rho t) for a constant rate rho under the model. The rate has inverse-time units, and convergence of an infinite-horizon objective also depends on the payoff's growth.
required_concepts: Exponential time discount with growth-dependent convergence.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any positive discount rate makes every infinitely growing payoff stream integrable.

cards.prompt: What is Present Value of a Flow? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The present value of a continuous flow is its time integral weighted by the specified discount factor. Horizon, time units, and convergence assumptions are needed; a flow value at one instant is not the entire accumulated value.
required_concepts: Discounted integral of a dated flow.
major_error_concepts: Treating an instantaneous payoff rate as a stock value without time integration.

cards.prompt: What is Optimal Control? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An optimal-control problem chooses a time path of controls to maximize an objective subject to state dynamics and constraints. States evolve according to the model, while controls are selected from the admissible set, with initial and terminal conditions specified.
required_concepts: Choose controls subject to state evolution and endpoint constraints.
major_error_concepts: Treating a state as freely selectable at every date while ignoring its evolution equation.

cards.prompt: What is Control Hamiltonian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For maximizing discounted payoff integral exp(-rho t)u(x,a) dt with xdot=f(x,a), a current-value Hamiltonian can be written H=u+lambda f. The costate weights the future consequence of changing the state, and conventions must match the accompanying equations.
required_concepts: Current payoff plus costate-weighted state dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Mixing a current-value Hamiltonian with present-value costate equations without adjustment.

cards.prompt: What is Costate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the stated current-value optimal-control convention, the costate obeys lambda dot=rho lambda-partial H/partial x under standard interior conditions. It describes the shadow value of the state, not necessarily a physical state variable or observed market price.
required_concepts: Current-value costate dynamics with discount term.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the rho lambda term while retaining the current-value convention for a discounted problem.

cards.prompt: What is Transversality Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A transversality condition restricts endpoint behavior in dynamic optimization according to the horizon, allowed endpoint variations, and state constraints. It rules out certain nonoptimal residual-value behavior, but no single formula applies unchanged to all infinite-horizon problems.
required_concepts: Endpoint optimality condition depends on the problem's constraints.
major_error_concepts: Imposing one memorized terminal formula on every constrained infinite-horizon model without checking its applicability.

cards.prompt: What is Bellman Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Bellman equation expresses optimal value as current reward plus discounted continuation value, optimized over feasible current actions. It relies on a state representation carrying the information needed for future decisions.
required_concepts: Recursive reward plus optimized continuation value.
major_error_concepts: Using a state that omits payoff-relevant history while claiming the same Markov recursion remains complete.

cards.prompt: What is Contraction Mapping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A contraction mapping brings pairs of inputs closer by a uniform factor below one in a specified complete metric space. Discounted Bellman operators can be contractions under boundedness and related assumptions, supporting a unique fixed point and iterative convergence.
required_concepts: Uniform shrinking in a complete space gives fixed-point control.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every Bellman operator is a contraction regardless of discounting, growth, or function space.

cards.prompt: What is Decision Rule? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A decision rule maps the current state or information to a feasible action in a dynamic model. It differs from a prewritten action sequence when later actions must respond to newly observed states.
required_concepts: State-dependent feasible action mapping.
major_error_concepts: Equating a feedback decision rule with one fixed sequence that ignores state changes.

cards.prompt: What is Value Iteration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Value iteration repeatedly applies a Bellman operator to an initial value function. Convergence is justified by the operator's properties and chosen function space, not by assuming that a numerically small update always proves the model was correctly specified.
required_concepts: Repeated recursive value updates with convergence conditions.
major_error_concepts: Calling apparent iteration stability proof that state discretization and economic assumptions are correct.

cards.prompt: What is Budget Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A budget constraint restricts expenditure to available resources under stated prices and timing. Intertemporal budgets additionally connect dated resources and choices through the model's saving, borrowing, or feasibility rules.
required_concepts: Resource-feasible expenditure relation with prices and timing.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring future repayment or feasibility obligations while calling present spending within an intertemporal budget.

cards.prompt: What is Payoff Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A payoff function assigns an objective value to choices and relevant states or other agents' actions. Its numerical scale and interpretation depend on whether it represents money, utility, or another criterion.
required_concepts: Objective value depends on choices and relevant context.
major_error_concepts: Adding utilities across agents as monetary amounts without an explicit interpersonal weighting model.

cards.prompt: What is Strategic Optimality Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a smooth strategic model, an interior best response can satisfy a first-order condition in an agent's own action while rivals' actions are held fixed. Equilibrium requires mutually compatible best responses and appropriate global or boundary checks.
required_concepts: Own-action optimality conditional on other actions.
Mutual compatibility and feasibility still needed.
major_error_concepts: Equating any simultaneous stationary conditions with a proven equilibrium without verifying each action is a best response.

cards.prompt: What is Cost-Minimization Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Cost minimization chooses a feasible input combination meeting an output requirement at minimum expenditure. Interior tangencies, boundary choices, and technological constraints must be handled with the appropriate constrained optimization conditions.
required_concepts: Minimize input expenditure subject to production feasibility.
major_error_concepts: Using an interior input-ratio tangency while ignoring a feasible cheaper corner.

cards.prompt: What is Utility-Maximization Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Utility maximization chooses a most-preferred affordable bundle under the stated utility representation and budget set. Increasing transformations preserve the chosen set but can change marginal units and numerical multipliers.
required_concepts: Maximize represented preferences subject to affordability.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the numerical magnitude of utility is uniquely determined by observed choices.

cards.prompt: What is Expected-Utility Risk Aversion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Within expected-utility theory, concave utility of wealth represents risk aversion over the specified domain because utility of the mean is at least expected utility. This is a model statement, not a complete psychological description of every risky choice.
required_concepts: Concavity and Jensen imply expected-utility risk aversion.
major_error_concepts: Inferring universal real-world risk behavior solely from one concave utility specification without its model assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Arrow-Pratt Measure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For increasing twice-differentiable utility, absolute risk aversion is -u double prime/u prime and relative risk aversion multiplies it by wealth. The measures are invariant to positive affine utility changes, not arbitrary increasing transformations of expected utility.
required_concepts: Arrow-Pratt absolute and relative curvature measures.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every nonlinear increasing utility transformation preserves the same expected-utility risk preferences.

cards.prompt: What is Certainty Equivalent? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A certainty equivalent solves u(CE)=E[u(X)] for an increasing utility function when the expectation and inverse are defined. For concave utility, CE is at most E[X], with risk premium E[X]-CE under the standard definition.
required_concepts: Sure outcome matching expected utility.
major_error_concepts: Equating certainty equivalent with expected payoff for every risk-averse nonlinear utility.

cards.prompt: What is Functional Form? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An economic functional form imposes a specific mathematical response structure, such as Cobb-Douglas multiplicative powers or a quadratic cost function. Its convenience brings restrictions on substitution, curvature, or scaling that should be interpreted as assumptions.
required_concepts: Chosen parametric form imposes substantive response restrictions.
major_error_concepts: Treating a convenient fitted formula as assumption-free evidence of all its structural properties.

cards.prompt: What is Identification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Identification asks whether distinct parameter values imply distinguishable model outcomes given the available observations and assumptions. A numerical optimizer returning one parameter vector does not establish that the parameters are uniquely identified.
required_concepts: Distinct parameter values must be distinguishable in model implications.
major_error_concepts: Claiming identification solely because software returns one numerical solution.

cards.prompt: What is Economic Units and Scaling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Units determine how mathematical economic quantities scale, such as a marginal cost measured in currency per output unit. Elasticities are dimensionless, while derivatives and multipliers generally carry units tied to the model variables.
required_concepts: Interpret derivatives and multipliers using their variable units.
major_error_concepts: Comparing raw coefficients measured in incompatible units as though their numerical sizes were directly meaningful.

cards.prompt: What is Numerical Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A numerical approximation replaces an exact mathematical operation with a finite computation, such as grid search, quadrature, or iterative root finding. Approximation error and convergence conditions remain separate from whether the economic model itself is appropriate.
required_concepts: Finite computation has numerical and model assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Treating one converged numerical output as proof of global optimum or correct economic specification without the relevant conditions.

cards.prompt: What is Sensitivity Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sensitivity analysis varies specified parameters or assumptions to examine how model outputs change. Local derivatives and larger scenario changes answer different questions, and robust-looking results only cover the variations actually considered.
required_concepts: Assess response to stated parameter and assumption changes.
major_error_concepts: Claiming invariance to all possible assumptions because a small selected parameter range produced similar outputs.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Mathematical Methods for Economics.
